name: consistency-violation-provider-below-element
description: A component rated BELOW an element it produces. The provider rule has no exemption and that asymmetry with the consumer rule is deliberate: a producer below what it produces is a mis-declaration, and no measure repairs it. A DERIVED `QM` counts — a component nothing allocates a level to, producing a rated element, is precisely the mis-declaration a safety engineer wants named.

context.summary: The bare `examples/basic` model: nothing declares an `asil` anywhere, so `ExampleSWC` derives QM. The change set rates `IExample.value`, which `ExampleSWC` provides through `pOut`, at ASIL D.

authorization.notes: The scope covers the address exactly, so the refusal is the model rule and not the authorization boundary. It is not the safety guard either: RAISING a level makes checks refuse more, so nothing here was ever offered to a host as a weakening. The consumer is not reported beside the provider, and the asymmetry is the rule's: `ExampleConsumerSWC` also derives QM, and a consumer BELOW the element it takes is not a finding at all — only one above it is.

input.intent: Rate the vehicle-speed signal at ASIL D.

expected.notes: Three addresses and three legal repairs the rule does not choose between: raise the component, lower the element, or change what the port is typed by. No requirement address appears, and the absence is informative — `ExampleSWC` derives its `QM` from a requirement that allocates nothing, so there is no levelled requirement to name. The consumer is not reported beside the provider: a component BELOW an element it takes is legitimate and only one above it is a finding, which is the asymmetry the two rules are built on.
